questions.prompt: What is the main focus of a mobile system design interview compared to a backend system design interview?

options.text: Client architecture, offline support, memory, battery, and flaky mobile networks
options.explanation: Right. Mobile interviews focus on client constraints, user experience, and modular iOS architecture.

options.text: Designing multi-region SQL database clusters and server load balancers
options.explanation: Server clusters and database sharding belong to backend system design interviews.

options.text: Building CI pipelines and choosing third-party analytics dashboards
options.explanation: Build pipelines and analytics tools are supporting setup, not the core client design.

options.text: Writing pixel-perfect SwiftUI animations for every screen layout
options.explanation: Visual polish is secondary to client architecture, caching, and system constraints.

questions.prompt: What should you do during the first 5 to 8 minutes of a 45-minute mobile system design interview?

options.text: Write full SwiftUI view layouts for every screen in the app.
options.explanation: Writing full UI layouts first wastes time before you know which features are in scope.

options.text: Clarify functional features, non-functional goals, and out-of-scope items.
options.explanation: Right. Scoping first makes sure you and the interviewer agree on what to design.

options.text: Pick third-party networking and database packages right away.
options.explanation: Choosing third-party packages comes after agreeing on core features and constraints.

options.text: Draw server database tables for all future company features.
options.explanation: Designing out-of-scope server tables uses up time needed for the mobile client.

questions.prompt: Which item is a functional requirement when designing a mobile news feed?

options.text: The feed scrolls smoothly at 60 frames per second.
options.explanation: Frame rate smoothness is a non-functional quality constraint.

options.text: The app limits disk cache usage to 100 megabytes.
options.explanation: Cache size limits are non-functional resource constraints.

options.text: Users can view posts, like a post, and pull to refresh.
options.explanation: Right. Functional requirements describe the core features and user actions in scope.

options.text: The app uses minimal battery during background sync.
options.explanation: Battery efficiency is a non-functional system quality.

questions.prompt: Which item is a non-functional requirement in a mobile system design interview?

options.text: Users can upload a new profile photo.
options.explanation: Uploading a photo is a functional user feature.

options.text: Users can tap a button to bookmark a post.
options.explanation: Bookmarking is a functional product feature.

options.text: Users can search posts by keyword.
options.explanation: Keyword search is a functional feature.

options.text: Recent posts stay readable offline without draining battery.
options.explanation: Right. Offline reliability and low battery drain are non-functional constraints.

questions.prompt: Why should you state out-of-scope features early in the interview?

options.text: To keep the design realistic inside 45 minutes and focus on key parts.
options.explanation: Right. Bounding scope prevents running out of time on secondary features like chat or video.

options.text: So you can skip explaining any non-functional requirements later.
options.explanation: Non-functional goals like offline support and smooth scrolling remain critical.

options.text: So the interviewer writes the API contract for you instead.
options.explanation: You still propose the API contract; scoping helps you focus on the right endpoints.

options.text: To avoid discussing caching, networking, or client architecture.
options.explanation: Scoping clears time specifically so you can focus on architecture and deep dives.

questions.prompt: What role does the Repository layer play in a clean mobile client architecture?

options.text: It renders SwiftUI animations on the GPU.
options.explanation: UI views handle rendering, while the Repository manages data sources.

options.text: It acts as a single source of truth between network and cache.
options.explanation: Right. The Repository hides whether data comes from memory, disk, or the API.

options.text: It replaces the ViewModel inside every screen.
options.explanation: The ViewModel prepares UI state and asks the Repository for domain data.

options.text: It holds SwiftUI view layouts and button tap handlers.
options.explanation: Views handle UI layout and taps, while the Repository manages data sources.

questions.prompt: Who is expected to pace the 45-minute mobile system design interview across the five steps?

options.text: Only the candidate, without checking in or adjusting for feedback.
options.explanation: You drive the pace, but you should check in so the interviewer can steer deep dives.

options.text: Only the interviewer, while the candidate waits silently for instructions.
options.explanation: Waiting passively makes it hard to evaluate senior ownership and communication.

options.text: The candidate, while checking in with the interviewer at each step.
options.explanation: Right. Good candidates drive the clock and confirm which deep dives the interviewer wants.

options.text: The interviewer alone, by grading a silent drawing at the end.
options.explanation: Mobile system design is an interactive conversation, not a silent drawing test.

questions.prompt: Why does a mobile feed API design often prefer cursor-based pagination over simple page numbers?

options.text: Cursor strings remove the need to cache any feed items locally.
options.explanation: Pagination controls page loading; local caching is still needed for offline support.

options.text: Page numbers work only with GraphQL and fail with REST APIs.
options.explanation: Both page numbers and cursors work over REST or GraphQL.

options.text: Cursors load the entire feed in one request without paging.
options.explanation: Cursor pagination still loads one page at a time using the next cursor.

options.text: Cursors avoid duplicate or skipped items when new posts arrive at the top.
options.explanation: Right. When new posts shift offsets, a cursor keeps the next page boundary accurate.

questions.prompt: Which step usually takes the most time (about 15 to 20 minutes) in a 45-minute mobile system design interview?

options.text: Deep dives into mobile bottlenecks like caching, offline sync, and pagination
options.explanation: Right. Deep dives show your real iOS engineering depth after scope and high-level design.

options.text: Listing functional requirements and out-of-scope features
options.explanation: Scoping should take about 5 to 8 minutes so plenty of time stays for design.

options.text: Sketching Swift protocol contracts and data models
options.explanation: Code contracts take about 5 minutes when asked.

options.text: Final wrap-up of trade-offs and production monitoring
options.explanation: The final wrap-up and trade-offs take about 3 to 5 minutes.

questions.prompt: Why is jumping straight into naming third-party libraries in minute one an interview trap?

options.text: Because third-party libraries never work in Release builds.
options.explanation: Many apps ship with libraries, but choosing tools before scoping misses the problem.

options.text: You may solve the wrong features and skip core requirements and trade-offs.
options.explanation: Right. Interviewers want to see how you scope constraints and reason about components first.

options.text: Because interviewers expect you to write your own HTTP engine first.
options.explanation: You can mention URLSession or standard layers, after scoping the problem.

options.text: Because third-party tools hide all client caching and offline choices.
options.explanation: Even with libraries, you must explain caching, pagination, and trade-offs first.

questions.prompt: When choosing between REST polling and WebSockets in Step 5, how should you present your choice?

options.text: Claim that WebSockets are always better in every mobile app.
options.explanation: WebSockets can drain battery faster when live updates are not required.

options.text: Avoid mentioning networking trade-offs completely.
options.explanation: Discussing trade-offs is a key part of Step 5.

options.text: Explain the trade-off, such as battery life versus real-time message freshness.
options.explanation: Right. Good answers state why a choice fits the constraints and what it gives up.

options.text: Say that REST and WebSockets have identical battery and server costs.
options.explanation: Keeping a persistent socket open has different battery and connection costs than periodic polling.

questions.prompt: During Step 5 (wrap-up), what should you mention alongside trade-offs to show production readiness?

options.text: Replacing every Swift protocol with a concrete class.
options.explanation: Removing protocols reduces testability and does not show production health.

options.text: Listing every Swift compiler flag in your Xcode project.
options.explanation: Compiler flags do not tell you how the app behaves for real users.

options.text: Disabling local caching on all user devices.
options.explanation: Disabling caching hurts offline support and increases data usage.

options.text: Monitoring crashes, launch time, and hang rates in production.
options.explanation: Right. Production monitoring shows how you check app health after shipping.

questions.prompt: In the 45-minute timeline diagram, what problem happens in the unstructured approach by minute 45?

options.text: Time runs out before discussing client caching, trade-offs, and monitoring.
options.explanation: Right. Without time-boxing, early tangents crowd out deep dives and trade-offs.

options.text: The candidate finishes in 5 minutes and skips drawing any diagram.
options.explanation: In the diagram, jumping straight into UI and backend details uses up the full 45 minutes.

options.text: The candidate spends all 45 minutes writing production SwiftUI tests.
options.explanation: In the diagram, jumping straight into UI boxes and backend servers uses up the time.

options.text: The candidate spends all 45 minutes on offline sync queues only.
options.explanation: The unstructured trap spends too long on UI boxes and backend servers.

questions.prompt: Why should your client architecture keep UI views and ViewModels decoupled behind a `FeedRepository` protocol?

options.text: Because `URLSession` cannot run inside async methods without a protocol.
options.explanation: URLSession supports async methods directly, but protocols keep layers separate.

options.text: So you can test ViewModels with stubs and swap cache or network logic cleanly.
options.explanation: Right. Protocol boundaries isolate UI state from storage and network details.

options.text: Because SwiftUI forbids ViewModels from holding arrays of model items.
options.explanation: ViewModels can hold arrays directly; protocols keep data sources easy to swap.

options.text: So the app skips creating any local disk or memory cache.
options.explanation: A Repository still uses memory and disk caches behind its protocol.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks you to design an offline-capable chat app, and you spend 25 minutes on server database sharding. What went wrong?

options.text: Offline chat apps do not use any local database on the phone.
options.explanation: Offline chat apps rely heavily on local persistence on the phone.

options.text: You focused too much on SwiftUI views instead of API design.
options.explanation: The problem was spending 25 minutes on server database sharding, not UI views.

options.text: You treated a mobile interview like a backend interview and skipped client design.
options.explanation: Right. Mobile interviewers evaluate client sync, storage, battery, and UI state.

options.text: You asked clarifying questions before drawing the architecture.
options.explanation: Asking clarifying questions is good; spending 25 minutes on server sharding is the trap.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: After sketching the high-level client architecture in Step 2, what is the best next move?

options.text: Stay quiet until the interviewer writes the deep-dive questions.
options.explanation: Waiting quietly breaks collaboration; you should lead the next transition.

options.text: Spend the remaining 30 minutes polishing SwiftUI colors and fonts.
options.explanation: Visual styling is out of scope compared to caching, sync, and pagination.

options.text: Jump straight to Step 5 trade-offs and end the interview early.
options.explanation: Deep dives (Step 3) are the biggest part of the interview and come before wrap-up.

options.text: Check in with the interviewer and ask which subsystem to deep-dive next.
options.explanation: Right. Checking in aligns your deep dive with what the interviewer wants to test.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, list the five main steps of a mobile system design interview in order.

rubric.criterion: Step 1: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements and scope
Step 2: Sketch high-level client architecture and API design
Step 3 and 4: Deep dive into key mobile subsystems and model code contracts
Step 5: Wrap up with trade-offs and monitoring

questions.modelAnswer: First, clarify functional features, non-functional constraints, and out-of-scope items. Second, sketch the high-level client architecture and API contract. Third, deep dive into hard mobile problems like caching, pagination, and offline sync. Fourth, model key code contracts if asked, and fifth, wrap up with explicit trade-offs and production monitoring.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain the difference between functional and non-functional requirements, and give one mobile example of each.

rubric.criterion: Defines functional requirements as user features/actions and gives a valid example
Defines non-functional requirements as quality/resource constraints and gives a valid mobile example

questions.modelAnswer: Functional requirements describe the core features and actions users can take, such as viewing a photo feed or liking a post. Non-functional requirements describe system quality and device constraints. For example, keeping scrolling smooth at 60 frames per second, supporting offline reading, or limiting battery and memory use are non-functional requirements.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain how a mobile system design interview differs from a backend interview. Cover client focus, device constraints, and client layers.

rubric.criterion: Explains that backend focuses on servers/databases/scaling while mobile focuses on the phone client
Names at least two concrete mobile constraints (unstable network, battery, memory/disk limits, offline support, smooth UI)
Mentions client architecture or modular layers (View, ViewModel, Repository, Cache)

questions.modelAnswer: A backend interview focuses on servers, load balancers, and database sharding, while a mobile interview focuses on the client app running on a user's phone. Mobile engineers must handle unstable cellular networks, offline reading, limited battery, and tight RAM limits. They also design clean client layers such as View, ViewModel, Repository, and local cache.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain why jumping into boxes or libraries in minute one is risky, and what to do instead.

rubric.criterion: Explains the risk: designing the wrong features or running out of time on out-of-scope details
States what to do instead: spend 5–8 minutes clarifying functional requirements, constraints, and out-of-scope items

questions.modelAnswer: Jumping straight into boxes or libraries is risky because you might design the wrong features. For example, you might design live video when the interviewer wanted an offline text feed. Instead, spend 5 to 8 minutes clarifying functional features, non-functional goals, and out-of-scope items.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain what makes a strong Step 5 wrap-up in a mobile system design interview.

rubric.criterion: Checks the final design against the requirements agreed in Step 1
States explicit trade-offs (e.g., battery vs freshness, memory vs out-of-memory crashes)
Mentions production monitoring (crash reports, launch time, or hang rates)

questions.modelAnswer: A strong Step 5 wrap-up checks that the design meets all functional and non-functional goals from Step 1. You state explicit trade-offs, such as saving battery with REST polling instead of live WebSockets. You also explain how you monitor production health through crash reports, launch time, and hang rates.
